questions.stem: A researcher shows that penicillin G efficiently kills a broth culture of Streptococcus pyogenes during log-phase growth but has almost no killing effect on the same organism held in stationary phase. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-lactamase output rises sharply in stationary phase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell wall synthesis occurs only in actively multiplying bacteria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Penicillins are bacteriostatic rather than bactericidal drugs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Porin channels close whenever bacterial growth slows

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ribosomal drug targets are exposed only in dividing cells

explanation.summary: Penicillins kill only during rapid growth, because only then is cell wall actively being built.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin action depends on the rapid growth of bacteria both in vitro and in vivo. For bacteria to grow, cell walls must be built; if cell wall synthesis is inhibited, growth is halted. These drugs are bactericidal, but they can only kill during rapid growth, when the organisms are actively multiplying.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nothing in the pharmacology of penicillins ties beta-lactamase output to growth phase; the explanation is the absence of wall synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillins are bactericidal, not bacteriostatic; the limitation is when they can kill, not whether they kill.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Porin changes are a resistance mechanism in some gram-negative rods, not a growth-phase phenomenon in a gram-positive coccus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillins do not act on the ribosome at all, so ribosomal target exposure is irrelevant.

questions.topicName: Penicillins

questions.stem: Penicillins are bactericidal at concentrations that are essentially nontoxic to human cells. Which of the following best explains this selective toxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human cells divide too slowly to be injured by the drug

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human cells exclude penicillin by means of efflux pumps

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human cells neither make nor require peptidoglycan

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human cells produce an intracellular beta-lactamase enzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human cells rapidly metabolize penicillin to an inert form

explanation.summary: Penicillins spare host cells because human cells have no peptidoglycan to target.
explanation.whyCorrect: The target of penicillins is the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the bacterial cell wall. Penicillins do not damage host cells because human cells neither make nor need peptidoglycan, so the drug has no equivalent target in the patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Growth rate of human cells is not the relevant factor; the absence of the drug target is.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Host efflux of the drug is not the described basis for selective toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-lactamase is a bacterial resistance enzyme, not a protective human enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillins are polar compounds that are not metabolized extensively; host metabolism is not the basis of their safety.

questions.topicName: Penicillins

questions.stem: Penicillin G, the antistaphylococcal penicillins, and the aminopenicillins differ from one another in spectrum, acid stability, and susceptibility to beta-lactamases, yet all are built on an identical bicyclic nucleus. These differences are produced mainly by modifying which portion of the molecule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The carbonyl carbon within the beta-lactam ring

choices.label: B
choices.text: The nitrogen atom within the beta-lactam ring

choices.label: C
choices.text: The side chain (R) group attached to the amide

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sulfur atom within the thiazolidine ring

choices.label: E
choices.text: The two methyl groups on the thiazolidine ring

explanation.summary: Penicillins differ chiefly in the R side chain of the amide group.
explanation.whyCorrect: Variation among the penicillins is mainly limited to the side chain (R) group of the amide. Altering this side chain is what changes acid stability, spectrum, and resistance to beta-lactamases across the subgroups. Separately, prodrugs have been developed by modifying the carboxylic acid group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The beta-lactam carbonyl is essential for binding transpeptidase and is not what is varied between agents.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The beta-lactam nitrogen is part of the ring that must stay intact for activity, not a site of structural variation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sulfur of the thiazolidine ring is part of the conserved nucleus shared by all penicillins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The two methyl groups on the thiazolidine ring are conserved features of the penicillin nucleus.

questions.topicName: Penicillins

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman with mild streptococcal pharyngitis is to be treated with an oral penicillin. Penicillin G is avoided in favor of penicillin V. Which property of penicillin V best accounts for this choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It covers the gram-negative rods that penicillin G misses

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has a far longer plasma half-life than penicillin G

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is more stable in gastric acid than penicillin G

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is not hydrolyzed by staphylococcal beta-lactamases

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reaches higher CSF concentrations than penicillin G

explanation.summary: Penicillin V is acid stable and therefore orally absorbed, whereas penicillin G is destroyed by gastric acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillins vary in their resistance to gastric acid and therefore in oral bioavailability. Penicillin G is poorly absorbed orally because it is broken down by gastric acid in the stomach, while penicillin V has increased absorption owing to its increased acid stability. That makes penicillin V the practical oral choice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Penicillin V shares the narrow gram-positive spectrum of penicillin G and has little activity against gram-negative rods.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma half-lives of most penicillins are similar, in the range of 30 minutes to 1 hour.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resistance to staphylococcal beta-lactamases belongs to the antistaphylococcal penicillins such as nafcillin and oxacillin, not to penicillin V.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillins cross into the CNS chiefly when the meninges are inflamed; penicillin V is not distinguished by CSF penetration.

questions.topicName: Penicillins

questions.stem: Most penicillins are eliminated unchanged by the kidney. One beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin is instead eliminated mainly in the bile, a point that matters when choosing an agent for a patient with poor renal function. Which of the following is that agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amoxicillin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ampicillin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin G

choices.label: E
choices.text: Piperacillin

explanation.summary: Nafcillin, a beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin, is excreted mainly in the bile.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin that resists staphylococcal beta-lactamases. Unlike the other penicillins, which are usually excreted unchanged in the urine by glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, nafcillin is mainly excreted in the bile. It also has poor oral absorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amoxicillin is an aminopenicillin, is not beta-lactamase resistant, and is renally eliminated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ampicillin is renally excreted; it is distinguished instead by undergoing enterohepatic recycling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin G is excreted unchanged in the urine and is readily hydrolyzed by beta-lactamases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Piperacillin is an antipseudomonal penicillin given parenterally and is not the biliary-excreted agent described.

questions.topicName: Penicillins

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with bacterial meningitis achieves therapeutic CSF concentrations on an intravenous penicillin. Once his meningeal inflammation resolves, the same dose would yield markedly lower CSF levels. Which of the following best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inflammation activates a pump that drives penicillin into the CSF

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inflammation allows penicillin to cross the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inflammation increases hepatic conversion of penicillin prodrug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inflammation sharply raises CSF protein binding of penicillin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inflammation slows the renal tubular secretion of penicillin

explanation.summary: Penicillins penetrate the CNS only when the meninges are inflamed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillins are widely distributed in the body, and most cross the blood-brain barrier to penetrate the central nervous system, but only when the meninges are inflamed. Once inflammation resolves, the barrier again restricts entry and CSF concentrations fall at any given dose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Active transport of penicillin at the CNS interface moves drug out of the CSF into the bloodstream, not into the CSF.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillins are polar compounds that are not metabolized extensively, so hepatic activation is not involved.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased CSF protein binding is not the described mechanism of CNS penetration for penicillins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal tubular secretion governs systemic elimination, not the ability of drug to enter the CSF.

questions.topicName: Penicillins

questions.stem: A patient with markedly reduced creatinine clearance is started on high-dose intravenous penicillin G and rapidly accumulates the drug. Which route of elimination normally handles this drug and accounts for the accumulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjugation with glucuronide and biliary export

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glomerular filtration and renal tubular secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 enzymes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrolysis by circulating plasma esterase enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestration and slow release from adipose tissue

explanation.summary: Penicillins are excreted unchanged in the urine by glomerular filtration and tubular secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillins are usually excreted unchanged in the urine via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion. They are polar compounds and are not metabolized extensively, so a fall in renal clearance directly raises drug concentrations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biliary excretion is the exception rather than the rule and applies chiefly to nafcillin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillins are not extensively metabolized, so hepatic oxidation is not the principal route of elimination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma esterase hydrolysis is not described as an elimination route for penicillins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillins are polar compounds and are not stored in fat.

questions.topicName: Penicillins

questions.stem: Among the penicillins, one agent is notable for being returned to the circulation after biliary excretion and reabsorption from the gut, a cycle that prolongs its intestinal exposure. Which of the following agents undergoes this enterohepatic recycling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ampicillin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxacillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin G

choices.label: E
choices.text: Penicillin V

explanation.summary: Ampicillin is the penicillin that undergoes enterohepatic recycling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin itself does not undergo enterohepatic recycling; it is ampicillin that does. Ampicillin is an aminopenicillin with increased stability to gastric acid, and it is also the penicillin most associated with nausea and diarrhea, consistent with prolonged exposure of the gut to drug.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Nafcillin is excreted mainly in the bile but is not the agent described as undergoing enterohepatic recycling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxacillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not associated with this cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin G is poorly absorbed orally and is excreted unchanged in the urine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillin V is distinguished by acid stability and good oral absorption, not by enterohepatic recycling.

questions.topicName: Penicillins

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is brought in for 3 days of right ear pain, irritability, and low-grade fever. Otoscopy shows a red, bulging tympanic membrane with decreased mobility on pneumatic otoscopy. Acute otitis media is diagnosed and antibiotic therapy is indicated. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amoxicillin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cefuroxime

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral vancomycin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical bacitracin

explanation.summary: Amoxicillin, with or without clavulanic acid, is the first-line antibiotic for acute otitis media.
explanation.whyCorrect: Otitis media is typically caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and susceptible Gram-negative bacteria. Amoxicillin is a broad-spectrum penicillin with good Gram-positive and Gram-negative coverage, which matches those organisms. It is listed as the first-line agent for otitis media, given with or without clavulanic acid.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cefuroxime is a second-generation cephalosporin with very limited Gram-positive coverage and is not the first-line choice here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin aimed at Staphylococcus aureus and is not used for otitis media.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral vancomycin is not absorbed and acts only in the gut; it is reserved for C. difficile infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bacitracin is a topical agent for minor skin wounds and has no role in middle ear infection.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl has fever, sore throat, and tender anterior cervical nodes. A throat culture grows Streptococcus pyogenes. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ceftaroline

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cefuroxime

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin VK

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vancomycin

explanation.summary: Oral penicillin (Penicillin VK) is the first-line agent for streptococcal pharyngitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillins have Gram-positive cocci coverage, and oral penicillin VK remains a useful first-line agent for many streptococcal infections. Pharyngitis due to Strep species is listed with oral penicillins as the first-line antibiotic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ceftaroline is reserved for MRSA and is not used for routine streptococcal pharyngitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cefuroxime is a second-generation cephalosporin and is not the first-line treatment for pharyngitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Streptococcus species are resistant to nafcillin, which was developed against staphylococci.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin does cover Gram-positive bacteria but is not first-line for pharyngitis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is scheduled for an elective open hernia repair. The surgical team wants an intravenous agent given before incision to cover Gram-positive cocci from the skin, with rapid bioavailability and peak tissue levels at the time of the incision. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amoxicillin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacitracin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cefazolin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ceftriaxone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cephalexin

explanation.summary: Cefazolin is the first-generation cephalosporin used intravenously for surgical prophylaxis through the skin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cefazolin is a first-generation cephalosporin given IV, so it is effective against the Gram-positive skin flora and reaches peak tissue levels rapidly at the time of incision. Surgical prophylaxis of procedures through the skin is listed with cefazolin as the first-line agent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amoxicillin is an oral broad-spectrum penicillin and does not provide rapid IV tissue levels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacitracin is a topical agent and cannot provide systemic prophylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ceftriaxone is a third-generation agent whose value is extended Gram-negative coverage, not skin prophylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cephalexin is also a first-generation cephalosporin but is oral, so it is not used for surgical prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has a warm, tender, erythematous plaque on her lower leg after a minor abrasion. There is no abscess, no fever, and no risk factors for resistant organisms. She will be treated as an outpatient with an oral agent. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cefoxitin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ceftazidime

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cephalexin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral vancomycin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated skin and soft tissue infections, typically due to Gram-positive cocci, are treated with a first-generation cephalosporin such as cephalexin.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-generation cephalosporins are primarily effective against Gram-positive bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus species, which are the usual causes of uncomplicated cellulitis. Cephalexin is the oral first-generation agent listed as first-line for these infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cefoxitin is a second-generation agent valued for Bacteroides coverage, not routine cellulitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ceftazidime is a third-generation agent used for extended Gram-negative coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral vancomycin is not absorbed from the gut and cannot treat a skin infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Piperacillin-tazobactam is a broad intravenous agent used when Pseudomonas coverage is needed.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old hemodialysis patient has fever and rigors. Blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cefazolin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cefepime

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin G

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vancomycin

explanation.summary: Vancomycin is one of the few antibiotics effective against MRSA and is first-line for MRSA infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vancomycin is effective against most Gram-positive organisms and is specifically one of the few agents that works against MRSA. MRSA infections are listed with vancomycin and ceftaroline as first-line treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cefazolin is a first-generation cephalosporin with good Gram-positive coverage but does not cover MRSA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cefepime retains good Gram-positive coverage except MRSA, so it would fail here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methicillin-resistant strains are by definition not susceptible to antistaphylococcal penicillins such as nafcillin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin G has limited activity because many staphylococci have developed resistance to penicillin.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man develops profuse watery diarrhea one week after completing a course of antibiotics. Stool testing confirms Clostridium difficile infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacitracin, topical

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ceftriaxone, intravenous

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nafcillin, intravenous

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vancomycin, intravenous

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vancomycin, oral

explanation.summary: Oral vancomycin is the drug of choice for Clostridium difficile infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vancomycin is one of the few antibiotics used to treat C. difficile infection, and the oral formulation is the drug of choice. Because oral vancomycin is not absorbed, it stays in the gut where the infection resides and acts essentially as a topical treatment there.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacitracin is a topical skin preparation and cannot treat a colonic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ceftriaxone does not treat C. difficile; broad cephalosporin use is the kind of exposure that precedes it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and has no role in C. difficile infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intravenous vancomycin does not cross into the gastric mucosa, so it would be ineffective for C. difficile.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications 1 – β-lactams and Vancomycin

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient with confirmed Clostridium difficile colitis is started on intravenous vancomycin. After several days the diarrhea is unchanged. Which of the following best explains the treatment failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C. difficile is a Gram-negative rod outside the drug's spectrum

choices.label: B
choices.text: C. difficile produces a β-lactamase that inactivates vancomycin

choices.label: C
choices.text: IV vancomycin does not cross into the infected gastric mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral vancomycin is absorbed systemically while the IV form is not

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vancomycin has no intrinsic activity against C. difficile organisms

explanation.summary: IV vancomycin has excellent systemic bioavailability but does not reach the gut mucosa, so it fails in C. difficile infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: An intravenous drug has essentially complete bioavailability and treats systemic infection well, but vancomycin given IV does not cross into the gastric mucosa. Because C. difficile resides primarily in that mucosa, the drug never reaches the organism, and only the oral formulation, which acts topically in the gut, is effective.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. difficile is a Gram-positive organism, and vancomycin covers most Gram-positive organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vancomycin is not a β-lactam, so β-lactamase production is not the issue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The relationship is reversed: oral vancomycin is essentially not absorbed at all.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin is in fact one of the few antibiotics active against C. difficile.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications 1 – β-lactams and Vancomycin

questions.stem: A patient with C. difficile colitis is prescribed vancomycin capsules by mouth. Which property of oral vancomycin makes this route appropriate for this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is absorbed and then concentrated into the bile

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is activated by first-pass hepatic metabolism

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is not absorbed, so it acts topically in the gut

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reaches high serum levels after an oral dose

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires gastric acid to convert to its active form

explanation.summary: Oral vancomycin has essentially zero bioavailability, so it stays in the gut and acts as a topical treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: When vancomycin is given orally it is not readily absorbed across the gastric mucosa, so its bioavailability is essentially zero. That failure of absorption is exactly what makes it useful: the drug remains at high concentration where C. difficile lives, acting as a local, topical therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biliary concentration is not the mechanism by which oral vancomycin reaches the colon.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vancomycin is not a prodrug requiring hepatic activation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral vancomycin produces almost no serum levels; IV dosing is required for systemic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin does not need gastric acid to become active.

questions.stem: Which generation of cephalosporins includes an agent with reliable activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fifth generation

choices.label: B
choices.text: First generation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fourth generation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Second generation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Third generation

explanation.summary: Fifth-generation cephalosporins, such as ceftaroline, are the ones active against MRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ceftaroline is the fifth-generation cephalosporin and is notable for activity against MRSA while maintaining broad-spectrum activity against Gram-negative bacteria. No earlier generation covers MRSA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: First-generation agents such as cefazolin and cephalexin cover Gram-positive organisms but explicitly not MRSA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fourth-generation cefepime retains good Gram-positive coverage except for MRSA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Second-generation agents have very limited Gram-positive coverage and no MRSA activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Third-generation agents extend Gram-negative coverage to Neisseria but do not cover MRSA.

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient with a suspected Gram-negative infection is switched from ceftriaxone to cefepime. Which of the following best describes cefepime?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fifth-generation agent with activity against MRSA

choices.label: B
choices.text: A first-generation agent with mainly Gram-positive activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: A fourth-generation agent with broader Gram-negative activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: A second-generation agent that also covers Bacteroides species

choices.label: E
choices.text: An antipseudomonal penicillin with anaerobic coverage

explanation.summary: Cefepime is a fourth-generation cephalosporin: good Gram-positive coverage except MRSA, with increased Gram-negative coverage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fourth-generation cephalosporins such as cefepime retain good Gram-positive coverage, with the exception of MRSA, while providing increased Gram-negative coverage compared with third-generation agents. That extra Gram-negative reach is the reason for switching from ceftriaxone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The fifth-generation agent active against MRSA is ceftaroline; cefepime does not cover MRSA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: First-generation agents are cefazolin and cephalexin, not cefepime.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The cephalosporins that cover Bacteroides are the second-generation agents cefoxitin and cefotetan.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Piperacillin-tazobactam, not cefepime, is the antipseudomonal penicillin with anaerobic coverage.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has dysuria and a purulent urethral discharge, and testing is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. A cephalosporin whose Gram-negative spectrum extends to Neisseria species is selected. Which of the following agents was chosen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacitracin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cefazolin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ceftriaxone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cephalexin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nafcillin

explanation.summary: Third-generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone extend Gram-negative coverage to Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin with a broad spectrum against Gram-positive bacteria and Gram-negative coverage extended beyond the first and second generations. That extended coverage specifically includes Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacitracin is a topical agent active against Gram-positive skin organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cefazolin is a first-generation agent with limited activity against Gram-negative bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cephalexin is the oral first-generation agent and also has limited Gram-negative activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin directed at Staphylococcus aureus.
