questions.stem: A patient is started on cefuroxime. Which of the following best describes this agent's generation and spectrum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fifth generation, with reliable activity against MRSA isolates

choices.label: B
choices.text: First generation, with coverage aimed mainly at Gram-positives

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fourth generation, with the broadest Gram-negative coverage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Second generation, with limited Gram-positive activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Third generation, with coverage extended to Neisseria species

explanation.summary: Cefuroxime is a second-generation cephalosporin with very limited Gram-positive coverage and better Gram-negative activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Second-generation cephalosporins such as cefuroxime, cefoxitin, and cefotetan have very limited Gram-positive coverage and are more effective against Gram-negative bacteria than the first-generation agents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ceftaroline is the fifth-generation agent with MRSA activity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The first-generation agents are cefazolin and cephalexin, which are primarily Gram-positive drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cefepime is the fourth-generation agent with the widest Gram-negative reach.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ceftriaxone and ceftazidime are the third-generation agents whose coverage includes Neisseria.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications 1 – β-lactams and Vancomycin

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a 2-day history of left flank pain, pain with urination, urinary frequency, and fever with occasional nausea. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), and she has left flank percussion tenderness; the remainder of the examination is normal. Acute pyelonephritis is diagnosed and ciprofloxacin is prescribed. This drug acts on which of the following bacterial targets?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dihydropteroate synthase in the folate pathway

choices.label: C
choices.text: DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin-binding transpeptidases of the cell wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolones inhibit the type II topoisomerases DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.
explanation.whyCorrect: All fluoroquinolones do effectively the same thing: they inhibit the type II topoisomerases DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, with variable specificity within the class. Loss of these enzymes halts DNA replication and kills the organism, which is why fluoroquinolones are bactericidal. Ciprofloxacin is a standard systemic fluoroquinolone used for urinary and other infections below the diaphragm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RNA polymerase is the target of rifamycins, not of fluoroquinolones.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dihydropteroate synthase is the target of the folic acid synthesis inhibitors, a different drug class.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transpeptidases are inhibited by β-lactams, which act on the cell wall rather than on DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 30S ribosomal subunit is bound by aminoglycosides and tetracyclines, which block protein synthesis.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: In the laboratory, a fluoroquinolone is added to purified bacterial DNA gyrase acting on plasmid DNA. The enzyme continues to cut the DNA backbone but the cut strands are no longer restored. Inhibition of which of the following enzyme domains best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ATPase domain that supplies energy for supercoiling

choices.label: B
choices.text: The helicase domain that separates parental strands

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ligase domain that reseals the nicked strand

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nuclease domain that nicks the DNA strand

choices.label: E
choices.text: The primase domain that lays down RNA primers

explanation.summary: Fluoroquinolones inhibit the ligase domain of type II topoisomerases while leaving the nuclease domain active.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV carry two kinds of domains: a nuclease domain that nicks a DNA strand so the DNA can untwist, and a ligase domain that repairs that nick. Fluoroquinolones target and inhibit the ligase domain, so the nuclease keeps nicking DNA with the repair mechanism removed. The enzyme is effectively converted into a DNA shredder.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An ATPase block would stop the enzyme altogether rather than leave unrepaired cuts accumulating.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Helicase is a separate replication enzyme and is not a domain of the type II topoisomerases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nuclease domain remains active; if it were inhibited, no cuts would be made at all.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primase synthesizes RNA primers and is not part of DNA gyrase or topoisomerase IV.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A microbiologist exposes a culture of Escherichia coli to levofloxacin. The bacterial chromosome accumulates unrepaired breaks, replication stops, and the organisms are killed rather than merely prevented from dividing. Which of the following best explains this bactericidal effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The drug binds the ribosome and causes misreading of messenger RNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug blocks DNA repair while the enzyme keeps cutting the DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the cell wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug inserts into the membrane and causes leakage of cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug prevents folate-dependent synthesis of thymidine for DNA

explanation.summary: Blocking the ligase domain turns type II topoisomerases into DNA shredders, halting replication and killing the cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because fluoroquinolones inhibit the repair (ligase) function while the nuclease continues to nick the DNA, the enzymes effectively shred the chromosome. DNA replication is halted and the bacterial cell dies, which explains the bactericidal nature of the class. This is distinct from bacteriostatic agents that merely stop growth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ribosomal misreading of mRNA is the mechanism of aminoglycosides and does not involve DNA breaks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peptidoglycan cross-linking is inhibited by β-lactams, a different class with a different target.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Membrane disruption with leakage of cytoplasmic contents describes agents such as polymyxins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Folate-dependent thymidine synthesis is blocked by the folic acid synthesis inhibitors, not by fluoroquinolones.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Bacterial type II topoisomerases perform several overlapping functions on the chromosome. Which of the following activities is unique to DNA gyrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cutting one DNA strand using an intrinsic nuclease domain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Introducing negative supercoils into the bacterial chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Relaxing negative supercoils that have formed in the DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resealing a cut DNA strand using an intrinsic ligase domain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Separating two completed daughter chromosomes from each other

explanation.summary: Only DNA gyrase can create negative supercoils, which offset the positive supercoiling generated by replication.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA gyrase uniquely creates negative supercoils, which help prepare the chromosome for the tension formed during DNA replication. When the strands of the helix are pulled apart, the DNA ahead winds tighter into positive supercoils, and gyrase counteracts this. Topoisomerase IV cannot introduce negative supercoils.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both gyrase and topoisomerase IV possess a nuclease domain that nicks DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Relaxation of negative supercoils is performed by topoisomerase IV and is shared by other topoisomerases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both gyrase and topoisomerase IV possess a ligase domain that repairs the nick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Separating completed daughter chromosomes is decatenation, the role of topoisomerase IV.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: At the end of replication a circular bacterial chromosome remains physically interlinked with its newly synthesized copy, and the two rings must be separated before the cell can divide. Which of the following enzyme activities accomplishes this separation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA gyrase introducing negative supercoils ahead of the fork

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helicase unwinding the parental duplex at the origin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligase sealing the Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primase synthesizing RNA primers on the leading strand

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase IV passing one strand through the other

explanation.summary: Decatenation of the two completed bacterial chromosomes is the distinctive role of topoisomerase IV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Topoisomerase IV plays a role in decatenation, that is, separating two completed bacterial chromosomes by passing one strand through the other. This progressively reduces the interlinking braids until the two rings are free. Fluoroquinolones that preferentially inhibit topoisomerase IV therefore block the final step of chromosome segregation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Negative supercoiling by gyrase manages torsional tension but does not unlink completed chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Helicase separates the two parental strands at the start of replication, not the finished daughter rings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ligase joins Okazaki fragments within a strand and cannot unlink two interlocked circles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primase lays down RNA primers to start synthesis and has no role in decatenation.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Fluoroquinolones take their name from the addition of a fluorine atom to an older core compound. Which of the following is the original quinolone, now no longer on the market?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Levofloxacin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Moxifloxacin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nalidixic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ofloxacin

explanation.summary: Nalidixic acid is the original, non-fluorinated quinolone and is no longer marketed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluoroquinolones are a fluorinated form of quinolone, their core component. Nalidixic acid is presented as an original quinolone that is no longer on the market, in contrast to ciprofloxacin, which is commonly prescribed. The fluorinated derivatives largely replaced it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ciprofloxacin is a fluorinated quinolone that remains one of the most commonly prescribed agents of the class.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Levofloxacin is a currently marketed fluoroquinolone and is the most commonly used respiratory agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Moxifloxacin is a currently marketed respiratory fluoroquinolone known for QTc prolongation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ofloxacin is a fluorinated quinolone still in use and is not the original core compound.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A patient with a severe gram-negative infection is treated with a β-lactam in addition to a fluoroquinolone, and the combination clears the infection more efficiently than either agent alone. Which of the following best explains this synergy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fluoroquinolone increases expression of the penicillin-binding proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fluoroquinolone inhibits the β-lactamases that would destroy the β-lactam

choices.label: C
choices.text: The β-lactam blocks the efflux pumps that export the fluoroquinolone

choices.label: D
choices.text: The β-lactam disrupts the cell wall so the fluoroquinolone enters more easily

choices.label: E
choices.text: The β-lactam raises intracellular pH so the fluoroquinolone stays ionized

explanation.summary: β-Lactams inhibit cell wall synthesis, which makes it easier for fluoroquinolones to enter the bacterium and reach their target enzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The efficiency of fluoroquinolones can be increased by using synergistic medications together. β-Lactam antibiotics inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis, allowing fluoroquinolones to have an easier time entering bacterial cells to reach their target enzymes. The two drugs therefore act at different steps that reinforce one another.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increasing penicillin-binding protein expression would not enhance fluoroquinolone activity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluoroquinolones act on type II topoisomerases and have no activity against β-lactamases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: β-Lactams do not inhibit the efflux pumps that bacteria use to export fluoroquinolones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Synergy is explained by easier entry through a damaged cell wall, not by an intracellular pH shift.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate that was previously susceptible now grows in the presence of ciprofloxacin. Intracellular drug concentrations are far lower than in the susceptible parent strain, while the sequences of the gyrase and topoisomerase IV genes are unchanged. Which of the following best accounts for the resistance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A point mutation in the gyrase subunit that binds the drug

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acetylation of the drug by a plasmid-encoded transferase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Active transport of the drug out of the cell by efflux pumps

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enzymatic cleavage of the drug by a bacterial hydrolase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the porin channels required for folate uptake

explanation.summary: One of the two main routes of fluoroquinolone resistance is efflux of the drug out of the bacterial cell by active transport.
explanation.whyCorrect: In general there are two main ways resistance develops to fluoroquinolones: active transport of the drug out of bacterial cells through efflux pumps, and alteration of the target binding site. A low intracellular concentration with a normal target sequence points to efflux. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is specifically noted as the most commonly resistant gram-negative organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A target mutation would leave intracellular drug levels normal, which is not what the assay shows.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetylating transferases inactivate aminoglycosides, not fluoroquinolones, and would not lower uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydrolytic destruction of the drug is not described as a mechanism of fluoroquinolone resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Porin loss affecting folate uptake is unrelated to fluoroquinolones, which do not act on folate synthesis.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Sequencing of a fluoroquinolone-resistant clinical isolate shows a chromosomal point mutation that changes an amino acid in a subunit of topoisomerase IV. Drug accumulation inside the bacterial cell is normal. Which of the following resistance mechanisms does this represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alteration of the drug's target binding site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased permeability of the outer membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inactivation of the drug by a bacterial enzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased export of the drug through efflux pumps

choices.label: E
choices.text: Overproduction of the drug's normal substrate

explanation.summary: Chromosomal mutation of a gyrase or topoisomerase IV subunit alters the target binding site and confers fluoroquinolone resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The second main route of resistance is alteration of the target binding site, specifically the topoisomerase IV or DNA gyrase subunits, by chromosomal mutation. The change can be chromosomal or integrated by way of plasmids acquired from nearby bacterial cells. Normal intracellular drug levels with an altered enzyme sequence identify this mechanism rather than efflux.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced outer membrane permeability would also lower intracellular drug, not leave it normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No drug-inactivating enzyme is implied, and drug levels inside the cell are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Efflux would reduce intracellular drug accumulation, which the assay shows is unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fluoroquinolones act on an enzyme rather than competing with a substrate that could be overproduced.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: An intensive care unit reports that fluoroquinolone resistance appeared in several unrelated gram-negative species within a few weeks of one another. Which of the following best explains how resistance spread so rapidly across different organisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of the antibiotic to an inactive metabolite by host enzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Independent spontaneous mutations arising in each separate species

choices.label: C
choices.text: Selection of pre-existing resistant clones by antibiotic pressure alone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transfer of plasmids carrying resistance genes between bacteria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vertical inheritance of resistance genes from parent to daughter cells

explanation.summary: Plasmids are little loops of genetic code acquired from nearby bacteria, and they let resistance spread quickly through a bacterial population.
explanation.whyCorrect: Target site alterations may be chromosomal or integrated by way of plasmids, small loops of genetic code acquired from nearby bacterial cells. Once one bacterium becomes resistant, the spread of resistance mechanisms via plasmids may quickly protect a large population. This horizontal transfer explains near-simultaneous resistance in unrelated species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Host metabolism of the antibiotic is a pharmacokinetic issue and is not a bacterial resistance mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Simultaneous independent mutation in several unrelated species within weeks is far less likely than plasmid spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Selection pressure alone does not explain how the same resistance determinant appears across species.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vertical inheritance passes genes only within a lineage and cannot cross between different species.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: Fluoroquinolone resistance is widespread among gram-positive organisms. Which of the following is the most frequent gram-positive culprit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Group A Streptococcus pyogenes from the pharynx

choices.label: B
choices.text: Listeria monocytogenes from food-borne exposure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium

explanation.summary: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequent gram-positive organism with fluoroquinolone resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Resistance to fluoroquinolones is unfortunately widespread among both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Among gram-positive organisms, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequent culprit. This is one reason fluoroquinolones are not relied on as monotherapy for suspected staphylococcal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Streptococcus pyogenes is not cited as a common source of fluoroquinolone resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Listeria monocytogenes is not named among the organisms driving fluoroquinolone resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. pneumoniae is the organism the respiratory fluoroquinolones are valued for covering, not the leading resistant gram-positive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enterococcus faecium is not identified as the most frequent gram-positive fluoroquinolone-resistant organism.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A hospital antibiogram shows that among gram-negative isolates, one organism accounts for the largest share of ciprofloxacin resistance. Which of the following is most likely that organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Escherichia coli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Haemophilus influenzae

choices.label: C
choices.text: Klebsiella pneumoniae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proteus mirabilis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa

explanation.summary: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most commonly fluoroquinolone-resistant gram-negative bacterium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among gram-negative bacteria, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most commonly resistant organism to fluoroquinolones. This matters clinically because levofloxacin is chosen among the respiratory fluoroquinolones partly for its better Pseudomonas coverage. Susceptibility testing is therefore important before relying on a fluoroquinolone for pseudomonal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escherichia coli is a common urinary pathogen but is not named as the most commonly resistant gram-negative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Haemophilus influenzae is not cited among the organisms driving fluoroquinolone resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klebsiella pneumoniae is not identified as the leading fluoroquinolone-resistant gram-negative organism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus mirabilis is not identified as the most commonly resistant gram-negative bacterium.

questions.topicName: DNA gyrase and Folic acid inhibitors– 2 of 2: Fluoroquinolones

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman has an 11-day history of facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, and fever. Examination shows maxillary sinus tenderness, and acute bacterial sinusitis is diagnosed. Which of the following groups of organisms is most likely responsible for her infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Proteus mirabilis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Listeria monocytogenes, Enterococcus faecalis, and Clostridioides difficile

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Rickettsia rickettsii

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Serratia marcescens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis

explanation.summary: Acute bacterial sinusitis is usually caused by S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and M. catarrhalis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute bacterial sinusitis is an upper respiratory tract infection, and the three organisms that classically cause it are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. This trio drives the choice of therapy, which must cover a gram-positive coccus plus two gram-negative respiratory organisms. Amoxicillin/clavulanate is therefore a very common treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These Enterobacteriaceae cause urinary and intra-abdominal infections, not the typical upper respiratory tract picture of sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Listeria, Enterococcus, and C. difficile cause meningitis, urinary tract infection, and colitis respectively, not sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These atypical and rickettsial organisms cause atypical pneumonia, genital infection, and tick-borne illness rather than bacterial sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These are hospital-associated gram-negative organisms seen in ventilated or severely ill patients, not causes of community sinusitis.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man is diagnosed with acute bacterial sinusitis and needs an oral antibiotic that will cover Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amoxicillin-clavulanate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gentamicin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Imipenem/cilastatin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linezolid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nafcillin

explanation.summary: Amoxicillin/clavulanate is the common treatment for acute bacterial sinusitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminopenicillins such as amoxicillin, when combined with a β-lactamase inhibitor like clavulanate, provide good gram-positive coverage plus good gram-negative coverage. That combination spans S. pneumoniae as well as H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis, which are the organisms of acute bacterial sinusitis. It is therefore a very common outpatient choice for this infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside with limited gram-positive activity and is not an oral agent for sinusitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbapenems are reserved for complicated infections such as hospital-acquired pneumonia and are not oral agents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Linezolid covers gram-positive organisms only and provides no coverage of the gram-negative respiratory pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin that is not effective against many gram-negative bacteria such as H. influenzae.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student is admitted with fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity. Cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci, and cultures grow Neisseria meningitidis. Which of the following antibiotics has activity against this organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ampicillin-sulbactam

choices.label: B
choices.text: Linezolid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral vancomycin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxacillin

explanation.summary: Ampicillin combined with sulbactam is effective against Neisseria meningitidis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminopenicillins paired with a β-lactamase inhibitor extend their reach into gram-negative organisms. Ampicillin with sulbactam is specifically effective against Neisseria meningitidis, which causes bacterial meningitis and septicemia. The other listed agents act only on gram-positive bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Linezolid is a gram-positive agent and would not treat a gram-negative diplococcus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not effective against many gram-negative bacteria, including Neisseria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral vancomycin is not absorbed, acts only in the gut, and has no gram-negative activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxacillin, like nafcillin, is aimed at staphylococci and lacks gram-negative coverage.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a urinary tract infection, and ampicillin is started. Aminopenicillins retain useful gram-positive activity with one important exception. Which of the following organisms is reliably covered by ampicillin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acinetobacter baumannii

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enterococcus faecalis

choices.label: C
choices.text: ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa

explanation.summary: Aminopenicillins cover gram-positive organisms including Enterococcus, but not MRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amoxicillin and ampicillin provide good gram-positive coverage, and Enterococcus is specifically included in that spectrum. The single gram-positive exception is MRSA, which aminopenicillins do not cover. Enterococcal urinary tract infection is therefore a classic ampicillin indication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acinetobacter is a resistant gram-negative organism outside the aminopenicillin spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing Enterobacteriaceae are explicitly not covered by aminopenicillins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MRSA is the named gram-positive exception to aminopenicillin coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aminopenicillins, even with a β-lactamase inhibitor, do not cover Pseudomonas.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 70-year-old hospitalized woman with a catheter-associated urinary tract infection is treated with ampicillin-sulbactam but remains febrile. Urine culture grows an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli. Which of the following best explains the treatment failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminopenicillins act only on organisms growing anaerobically

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aminopenicillins are excreted unchanged and never reach the urine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aminopenicillins cover only atypical intracellular pathogens

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aminopenicillins do not cover ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aminopenicillins inhibit the 30S ribosome rather than the cell wall

explanation.summary: Aminopenicillins fail against ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae and against Pseudomonas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amoxicillin and ampicillin, even with a β-lactamase inhibitor, do not cover extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing Enterobacteriaceae or Pseudomonas. ESBL organisms make β-lactamase enzymes that degrade these β-lactam antibiotics. Carbapenems are the reliable option once an ESBL producer is identified.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminopenicillins are not restricted to anaerobic growth conditions; E. coli grows aerobically and is ordinarily within their spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Drug delivery to the urine is not the problem here; enzymatic degradation of the antibiotic is.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aminopenicillins with an inhibitor cover many atypicals but are not limited to them; they are primarily cell-wall active agents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aminopenicillins are β-lactams that block cell wall synthesis; 30S inhibition describes aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man in the intensive care unit develops fever and hypotension three days after abdominal surgery. Broad empiric coverage of gram-positive organisms, Enterobacteriaceae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is needed while cultures are pending. Which of the following single agents is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ampicillin-sulbactam

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aztreonam

choices.label: C
choices.text: Doxycycline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam has one of the broadest gram-negative spectra and is used for initial empiric therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Piperacillin-tazobactam has broad gram-positive coverage (except MRSA) together with one of the broadest gram-negative coverages, including Enterobacter, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Serratia, Proteus, ESBL producers, and Pseudomonas. That breadth is exactly why it is chosen for initial empiric therapy in a septic post-surgical patient. No other listed agent spans gram-positives and Pseudomonas at once.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ampicillin-sulbactam does not cover Pseudomonas or ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aztreonam treats only aerobic gram-negative bacteria and would leave gram-positive organisms uncovered.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxycycline is not effective against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and has limited activity against anaerobes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin with no meaningful gram-negative activity.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A patient with a complicated intra-abdominal infection is receiving piperacillin-tazobactam, and cultures return a gram-negative bacillus. Which of the following organisms is expected to be covered by this agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Klebsiella pneumoniae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rickettsia rickettsii

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam covers Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli, Klebsiella, Serratia, and Proteus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond its broad gram-positive coverage, piperacillin-tazobactam covers gram-negative organisms including Enterobacter species, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Serratia, and Proteus. Klebsiella pneumoniae therefore falls squarely within its spectrum. This is part of why it is a workhorse empiric agent for intra-abdominal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MRSA is the stated gram-positive exception to piperacillin-tazobactam coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycoplasma is an atypical pathogen treated with doxycycline, not with a β-lactam.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rickettsial organisms are treated first-line with doxycycline and are not covered by β-lactams.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus is not within its spectrum; tetracyclines are the class credited with VRE activity.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with a severe skin and soft tissue infection is receiving piperacillin-tazobactam but remains febrile. Blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following best explains the inadequate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Escherichia coli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Klebsiella species

choices.label: C
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against MRSA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Proteus species

choices.label: E
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam lacks activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam has broad gram-positive coverage except for MRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Piperacillin-tazobactam's gram-positive coverage is broad but explicitly excludes MRSA. When MRSA is isolated, an anti-MRSA agent must be used instead of relying on the β-lactam. Its gram-negative reach, by contrast, is one of the broadest available.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escherichia coli is covered by piperacillin-tazobactam.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Klebsiella is within its gram-negative spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus is among the gram-negative organisms it covers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Piperacillin-tazobactam does cover Pseudomonas, which is one of its main advantages.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man is hospitalized with bloody diarrhea and bacteremia, and blood cultures grow Campylobacter. Which of the following agents provides coverage of this organism in addition to broad gram-positive and gram-negative coverage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Linezolid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral vancomycin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxacillin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam

explanation.summary: Piperacillin-tazobactam's broad spectrum includes Pseudomonas and Campylobacter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Piperacillin-tazobactam has broad gram-positive coverage (except MRSA) and very broad gram-negative coverage that includes Pseudomonas and Campylobacter. That breadth makes it suitable for initial empiric therapy in a septic patient before the organism is known. The other options are gram-positive agents or narrow penicillins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Linezolid is a gram-positive agent and would not treat a gram-negative enteric organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not effective against many gram-negative bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral vancomycin is not absorbed, works only in the gut lumen, and has no gram-negative activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxacillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin aimed at gram-positive cocci, not enteric gram-negative rods.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: Blood cultures from a 66-year-old woman with pyelonephritis grow an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae. Which of the following agents is the most reliable treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Linezolid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Meropenem

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nafcillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penicillin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vancomycin

explanation.summary: Carbapenems are the most reliable treatment for ESBL-producing bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbapenems are considered the most reliable treatment for infections caused by extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing organisms. Their broad-spectrum activity and stability against β-lactamase enzymes is what preserves activity when other β-lactams are degraded. Meropenem is the only carbapenem among the options.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Linezolid covers gram-positive organisms and has no activity against a gram-negative bacillus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nafcillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not effective against gram-negative bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin is readily degraded by β-lactamases and lacks the needed gram-negative spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vancomycin has no gram-negative coverage at all.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: An Escherichia coli isolate from a hospitalized patient is resistant to ampicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and several cephalosporins but remains susceptible to meropenem. Which of the following best explains this resistance pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The organism grows only under anaerobic conditions

choices.label: B
choices.text: The organism has acquired a thick polysaccharide capsule

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism has lost its peptidoglycan cell wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism has mutated its 30S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism produces extended-spectrum β-lactamase enzymes

explanation.summary: ESBL producers make enzymes that degrade β-lactam antibiotics, leaving carbapenems as the reliable option.
explanation.whyCorrect: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing bacteria secrete β-lactamase enzymes that degrade other β-lactam antibiotics, which explains resistance across penicillins and cephalosporins. Carbapenems combine broad-spectrum activity with resistance to these enzymes, so they remain active. That is why carbapenems are the most reliable therapy for ESBL infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli is a facultative organism, and anaerobic growth does not explain β-lactam degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A capsule impairs phagocytosis but does not selectively inactivate β-lactam antibiotics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of the cell wall is not a feature of E. coli and would not spare carbapenem activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 30S mutation would affect aminoglycosides and tetracyclines, not β-lactams.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: Carbapenems are often summarized as covering essentially all gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Which of the following organisms is the important gram-positive exception to that rule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-lactamase-producing Haemophilus influenzae

choices.label: B
choices.text: ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Carbapenems cover a wide range of gram-positive and gram-negative organisms except MRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The shorthand for carbapenems is that they cover all gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, but MRSA is the explicit gram-positive exclusion. Anti-MRSA therapy must be added when that organism is suspected or isolated. The rest of the gram-positive and gram-negative spectrum is broad.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Haemophilus influenzae is a gram-negative organism covered by carbapenems, not the exception.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ESBL-producing Klebsiella is precisely the organism carbapenems treat most reliably.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methicillin-susceptible S. aureus is a gram-positive organism well within the carbapenem spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pneumoniae is covered by the broad gram-positive activity of carbapenems.

questions.topicName: Spectrum of Activity and Indications – 2: β-lactams and 30S Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted with a pyogenic infection. The team selects a protein synthesis inhibitor. Under which condition are protein synthesis inhibitors most effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When host phagocytes have already engulfed most of the organisms

choices.label: B
choices.text: When the bacteria are actively dividing during acute infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: When the infection has become chronic and walled off by fibrosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: When the organism has formed a mature biofilm on a foreign body

choices.label: E
choices.text: When the organisms have entered a dormant, non-replicating state

explanation.summary: Protein synthesis inhibitors work best during the acute stage of infection, when bacteria are actively dividing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protein synthesis inhibitors act on the bacterial ribosome, so their effect depends on ongoing translation. Actively dividing organisms are synthesizing protein at a high rate and are therefore maximally susceptible. This is why these drugs are most effective during the acute stage of an infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phagocytosis is a host clearance mechanism and is not the condition that determines protein synthesis inhibitor efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A chronic, walled-off focus contains slowly metabolizing organisms and is the opposite of the acute stage favored here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Biofilm organisms are metabolically slowed and shielded, which reduces rather than enhances the effect of these agents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dormant, non-replicating organisms are translating minimally, so ribosome-directed drugs have little to act on.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A student is learning bacterial translation and notes that the ribosome contains three defined positions where individual amino acids are loaded and bonded, designated A, P, and E. Which set of names corresponds to these three letters?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acceptor, peptidyl, and elongation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Activation, polymerase, and extension

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anchor, priming, and exchange

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anticodon, primer, and editing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Attachment, processing, and excision

explanation.summary: The three ribosomal sites are A (acceptor), P (peptidyl), and E (elongation).
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacterial ribosomes contain three sites important for peptide synthesis: A = acceptor, P = peptidyl, and E = elongation. Individual amino acids are loaded and bonded at these positions. Protein synthesis inhibitors act by interacting with these sites or with other parts of the ribosomal subunits.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Activation, polymerase, and extension describe other biochemical concepts, not the A, P, and E positions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anchor, priming, and exchange do not correspond to any of the three defined ribosomal sites.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticodon, primer, and editing are not the names given to the three ribosomal sites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Attachment, processing, and excision are unrelated to the acceptor, peptidyl, and elongation sites.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: An investigator studies an antibiotic whose target lies within the small subunit of the bacterial ribosome. That subunit is built from a single ribosomal RNA molecule together with 21 associated proteins. Which ribosomal RNA is present in this subunit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 5S ribosomal RNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: 16S ribosomal RNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: 18S ribosomal RNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: 23S ribosomal RNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: 28S ribosomal RNA

explanation.summary: The prokaryotic 30S subunit is composed of 16S rRNA plus 21 other proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The small ribosomal subunit in bacteria is the 30S subunit, and it is made up of 16S rRNA and 21 additional proteins. Aminoglycosides act at the 30S subunit and specifically target this 16S rRNA. Enzymatic modification of aminoglycosides prevents their interaction with the 16S rRNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5S rRNA is a component of the large 50S subunit, not the small subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 18S rRNA is a eukaryotic ribosomal RNA and is not part of the bacterial small subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 23S rRNA belongs to the 50S subunit and carries peptidyl transferase activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 28S rRNA is a eukaryotic ribosomal RNA and is not found in bacterial ribosomes.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: The large subunit of the 70S bacterial ribosome is responsible for forming the peptide bond between successive amino acids during protein synthesis. Which ribosomal RNA molecules compose this subunit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 16S rRNA and 23S rRNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: 16S rRNA and 5S rRNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: 23S rRNA and 28S rRNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: 23S rRNA and 5S rRNA

explanation.summary: The 50S subunit is composed of 23S rRNA and 5S rRNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: In prokaryotes the large subunit is the 50S subunit, composed of 23S rRNA and 5S rRNA. It is the subunit important for forming the peptide bond between amino acids in protein synthesis. The 23S rRNA within it contains peptidyl transferase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 16S rRNA belongs to the small subunit, so this pairing spans two different subunits.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 16S rRNA is a component of the 30S small subunit, not of the large subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 18S and 28S rRNA are eukaryotic ribosomal RNAs and are absent from bacterial ribosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 28S rRNA is eukaryotic, so it cannot be part of the bacterial 50S subunit.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A bacterial mutant binds incoming charged tRNAs normally but cannot join successive amino acids into a growing polypeptide chain. The defect maps to the ribosomal RNA that carries peptidyl transferase activity. Which molecule is defective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 16S rRNA of the 30S subunit

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 5S rRNA of the 50S subunit

choices.label: D
choices.text: The initiator tRNA of the initiation complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: The messenger RNA at the acceptor site

explanation.summary: Peptidyl transferase, the enzyme that forms peptide bonds, resides in the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 23S rRNA contains peptidyl transferase, the enzyme that forms the peptide bonds between amino acids. A defect there permits tRNA binding but prevents bond formation. Chloramphenicol produces the same functional block by preventing transpeptidation at the 50S subunit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 16S rRNA is in the small subunit and is involved in decoding, not in peptide bond formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 5S rRNA is part of the 50S subunit but is not the molecule that carries peptidyl transferase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The initiator tRNA participates in initiation complex formation rather than in transpeptidation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Messenger RNA carries the coding sequence and has no catalytic role in peptide bond formation.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A medicinal chemist describes a class of antibacterial agents constructed from two or more amino sugars linked to a central aminocyclitol nucleus, with individual members differing in the amino sugars they carry. Which antibiotic class is described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminoglycosides

choices.label: B
choices.text: Macrolides

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxazolidinones

choices.label: D
choices.text: Streptogramins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tetracyclines

explanation.summary: Aminoglycosides are composed of two or more amino sugars bonded to an aminocyclitol nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Structurally, aminoglycosides consist of two or more amino sugars bonded to an aminocyclitol nucleus, and the various aminoglycosides differ in which amino sugars they carry. These sugar moieties make the agents very hydrophilic, which is why they must be given intravenously.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrolides carry the suffix '-mycin' and include azithromycin, clarithromycin, and erythromycin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxazolidinones are represented by linezolid and are structurally unrelated to amino sugars.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Streptogramins comprise dalfopristin and quinupristin and do not share this aminocyclitol structure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tetracyclines are named for their four-ring structure and end in the suffix '-cycline', not for amino sugars.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a health care-associated gram-negative infection is to be started on an aminoglycoside. Which of the following drugs belongs to that class?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clindamycin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Doxycycline

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erythromycin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linezolid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tobramycin

explanation.summary: Tobramycin is an aminoglycoside, alongside streptomycin, neomycin, gentamicin, and amikacin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Common examples of aminoglycosides include streptomycin, neomycin, gentamicin, tobramycin, and amikacin. All are 30S protein synthesis inhibitors. Because their structure contains sugar moieties they are very hydrophilic and are administered intravenously.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clindamycin is a lincosamide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Doxycycline is a second-generation tetracycline, a different 30S protein synthesis inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythromycin is a macrolide, identified by the '-mycin' suffix, acting at the 50S subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Linezolid is an oxazolidinone that binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: An intern asks why gentamicin cannot simply be prescribed as a tablet for an outpatient. Which property of aminoglycosides best explains the need for parenteral administration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dietary calcium chelates them within the gastric lumen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism removes them rapidly

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gastric acid degrades them into inactive ring fragments

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gut peptidases destroy them before absorption occurs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their sugar moieties make them hydrophilic and poorly absorbed

explanation.summary: Aminoglycosides are highly hydrophilic because of their sugar moieties, so they are absorbed poorly and given IV or IM.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because their structure contains sugar moieties, aminoglycosides are very hydrophilic. Poor oral absorption follows, so these agents are administered intravenously or intramuscularly. They are then eliminated unchanged by the kidneys.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chelation by dietary cations is not the mechanism given for the parenteral route of aminoglycosides.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The 30S ribosomal inhibitors are not substantially metabolized, so first-pass metabolism does not explain this.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acid degradation is not the stated limitation; poor absorption of a hydrophilic molecule is.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aminoglycosides are not peptides, and proteolysis in the gut is not the reason they are given parenterally.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: Tetracyclines were originally valued for broad-spectrum activity, but bacterial resistance eroded that advantage. Agents with greater antibacterial properties were then developed and remain widely used today. Which pair represents these second-generation tetracyclines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Azithromycin and clarithromycin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dalfopristin and quinupristin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Doxycycline and minocycline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Streptomycin and neomycin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tobramycin and amikacin

explanation.summary: Doxycycline and minocycline are the second-generation tetracyclines developed in response to resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tetracyclines end in '-cycline' and were known for broad-spectrum activity. As bacteria developed resistance, the second-generation agents doxycycline and minocycline were developed with greater antibacterial properties and are still widely used today.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azithromycin and clarithromycin are macrolides that act at the 50S subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dalfopristin and quinupristin are streptogramins that act synergistically at the 50S subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Streptomycin and neomycin are aminoglycosides, not tetracyclines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tobramycin and amikacin are aminoglycosides composed of amino sugars.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with community-acquired atypical pneumonia is treated with a macrolide. Which of the following agents is a macrolide?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amikacin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Azithromycin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chloramphenicol

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clindamycin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Linezolid

explanation.summary: Macrolides carry the suffix '-mycin' and include azithromycin, clarithromycin, and erythromycin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The macrolides are 50S protein synthesis inhibitors identified by the suffix '-mycin' and include azithromycin, clarithromycin, and erythromycin. They interfere with protein elongation by binding reversibly to the 50S ribosomal subunit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amikacin is an aminoglycoside that acts at the 30S subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chloramphenicol is its own agent that binds the 50S subunit and prevents transpeptidation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clindamycin is a lincosamide, a separate class that also binds the 50S subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Linezolid is an oxazolidinone that binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with an anaerobic soft-tissue infection is treated with clindamycin. To which antibiotic class does clindamycin belong, and which ribosomal subunit does it bind?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminoglycoside; 30S subunit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincosamide; 50S subunit

choices.label: C
choices.text: Macrolide; 50S subunit

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxazolidinone; 50S subunit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tetracycline; 30S subunit

explanation.summary: Clindamycin is the lincosamide among the 50S protein synthesis inhibitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 50S protein synthesis inhibitors comprise macrolides, the lincosamide clindamycin, streptogramins, and oxazolidinones. Clindamycin binds reversibly to the 50S ribosomal subunit and, like the macrolides, interferes with protein elongation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminoglycosides are amino sugar compounds acting at the 30S subunit and 16S rRNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrolides are the '-mycin' agents azithromycin, clarithromycin, and erythromycin, not clindamycin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The oxazolidinone class is represented by linezolid, a different 50S agent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tetracyclines end in '-cycline' and bind the 30S subunit, which does not describe clindamycin.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with a resistant gram-positive bloodstream infection is given linezolid. Linezolid is the representative member of which antibiotic class?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminoglycosides

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincosamides

choices.label: C
choices.text: Macrolides

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxazolidinones

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptogramins

explanation.summary: Linezolid is an oxazolidinone and one of the 50S protein synthesis inhibitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oxazolidinones, represented by linezolid, are important members of the 50S protein synthesis inhibitors. Linezolid binds the 23S ribosomal RNA of the 50S subunit at the interphase of the 30S and 50S subunits to prevent initiation complex formation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminoglycosides are 30S inhibitors built from amino sugars, such as gentamicin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lincosamide class is represented by clindamycin, not linezolid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrolides carry the '-mycin' suffix and include azithromycin and erythromycin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptogramins are dalfopristin and quinupristin, which are given together for synergy.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitor-1 of 2: Mechanisms of Action

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with gram-negative bacteremia completes a 10-day course of an intravenous antibiotic. Two weeks later he reports persistent high-frequency hearing loss and constant ringing in both ears. Which of the following antibiotics is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amikacin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clindamycin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Doxycycline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linezolid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quinupristin/dalfopristin

explanation.summary: Ototoxicity is one of the two classic adverse reactions of the aminoglycosides.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amikacin is an aminoglycoside, and nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity are the two common adverse reactions of this class. The drug accumulates in cochlear cells, where inhibition of mitochondrial ribosomes causes cell death. Because cochlear cells cannot regenerate, the resulting hearing loss is irreversible.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Clindamycin causes diarrhea, allergic reaction and neuromuscular blockade, and is linked to pseudomembranous colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxycycline is a tetracycline; its characteristic adverse effects are GI upset, photosensitivity and tooth discoloration, not ototoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Linezolid most characteristically causes bone marrow suppression, peripheral neuropathy and serotonin syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Quinupristin/dalfopristin is a streptogramin, and its hallmark adverse effect is arthralgia/myalgia.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitors–2 of 2: Adverse Drug Reaction

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman receiving gentamicin for 8 days has a rise in serum creatinine from 0.9 mg/dL to 2.1 mg/dL. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts consistent with acute tubular necrosis. Which of the following best explains this drug's renal toxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It constricts the afferent arteriole and lowers glomerular filtration pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is filtered at the glomerulus and accumulates within proximal tubular cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It obstructs the collecting ducts with pigmented protein casts

choices.label: D
choices.text: It precipitates as insoluble crystals within the distal tubular lumen

choices.label: E
choices.text: It triggers an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction in the renal interstitium

explanation.summary: Aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity is proximal tubular accumulation leading to acute tubular necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminoglycosides are able to filter across the glomerulus and then accumulate in the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule. That accumulation increases the permeability of those cells, which can lead to acute tubular necrosis. This is why creatinine and urine sediment are monitored during therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminoglycosides are not described as causing renal injury through afferent arteriolar constriction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pigment cast obstruction describes myoglobinuric injury, not aminoglycoside toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Crystal precipitation in the tubular lumen is not the mechanism described for aminoglycosides.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The injury is a direct toxic tubular effect, not an allergic interstitial reaction.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitors–2 of 2: Adverse Drug Reaction

questions.stem: Two patients are started on the same weight-based dose of gentamicin: a 25-year-old man with normal renal function and an 80-year-old woman with a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min. The older patient is judged to be at substantially higher risk of nephrotoxicity. Which of the following best accounts for this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminoglycoside plasma protein binding is markedly higher in older adults

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elderly patients absorb a much greater fraction of each intramuscular dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elderly patients convert aminoglycosides into a nephrotoxic metabolite

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elderly patients have higher renal clearance of aminoglycosides

choices.label: E
choices.text: Impaired renal function and advanced age both raise aminoglycoside nephrotoxic risk

explanation.summary: Aminoglycoside nephrotoxic risk rises with impaired renal function and with older age.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states explicitly that the nephrotoxicity risk of aminoglycosides increases with impaired renal function and in the elderly. Both features apply to the older patient, so the same dose carries a higher risk of tubular accumulation and acute tubular necrosis for her.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Altered protein binding is not given as the reason for the increased risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased intramuscular absorption with age is not a described risk factor for this toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aminoglycoside toxicity is attributed to accumulation of the drug itself, not to a metabolite.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal clearance falls rather than rises with age and renal impairment.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitors–2 of 2: Adverse Drug Reaction

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman treated with amikacin develops bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Six months after the drug was stopped, repeat audiometry shows no improvement. Which of the following best explains the permanence of this deficit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminoglycosides permanently occlude the cochlear blood supply

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cochlear cells that have been killed are unable to regenerate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cochlear damage is sustained by an ongoing autoimmune response

choices.label: D
choices.text: The deficit reflects irreversible injury to the auditory cortex

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug remains irreversibly bound to cochlear ribosomes for years

explanation.summary: Aminoglycoside hearing loss is permanent because cochlear cells cannot regenerate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ototoxicity is caused by inhibition of mitochondrial ribosomes in cochlear and vestibular cells, resulting in cell death. Cochlear cells are unable to regenerate, so once they are lost the hearing loss is irreversible. This contrasts with the vestibular deficits, which are sometimes reversed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vascular occlusion of the cochlea is not the described mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No autoimmune mechanism is described for aminoglycoside ototoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lesion is in the cochlear hair cells of the inner ear, not in the auditory cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick attributes the permanence to cell death and failed regeneration, not to persistent drug binding.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitors–2 of 2: Adverse Drug Reaction

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man treated with gentamicin develops disequilibrium and unsteady gait along with hearing loss. Over the following months his balance gradually improves, although his hearing remains unchanged. Which of the following best explains the improvement in his balance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aminoglycosides are cleared from vestibular tissue within hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: The balance symptoms were caused by a transient electrolyte shift

choices.label: C
choices.text: The vestibular nerve is shielded from the drug by the blood-labyrinth barrier

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vestibular cells are able to regenerate after they are injured

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vestibular cells are not affected by aminoglycoside exposure

explanation.summary: Vestibular cells can regenerate, so aminoglycoside balance deficits are sometimes reversible.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminoglycosides kill both cochlear and vestibular cells by inhibiting mitochondrial ribosomes. Unlike cochlear cells, vestibular cells can regenerate, and balance deficits are therefore sometimes reversed. The cochlear loss in the same patient remains permanent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rapid clearance from the tissue is not the reason given for recovery.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The deficit is due to drug-induced vestibular cell death, not an electrolyte disturbance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The vestibular apparatus is clearly exposed to the drug, as shown by the symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vestibular cells are directly affected; that is why the patient became unsteady in the first place.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitors–2 of 2: Adverse Drug Reaction

questions.stem: A researcher exposes cultured cochlear hair cells to increasing concentrations of gentamicin and observes progressive cell death. Which of the following intracellular targets is most directly responsible for this toxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lysosomal proton pumps

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mitochondrial ribosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nuclear DNA topoisomerase II

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plasma membrane sodium channels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sarcoplasmic calcium ATPase

explanation.summary: Aminoglycoside ototoxicity comes from inhibition of mitochondrial ribosomes in inner ear cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ototoxicity is caused by inhibition of mitochondrial ribosomes in cochlear and vestibular cells, which results in cell death. Mitochondrial ribosomes resemble the bacterial ribosomes these drugs are designed to target, which is why host inner ear cells are vulnerable.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lysosomal proton pumps are not the target described for aminoglycoside inner ear toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Topoisomerase inhibition is not a mechanism attributed to aminoglycosides.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sodium channel blockade is unrelated to aminoglycoside cochlear injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcium ATPase inhibition is not described as the basis of ototoxicity.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitors–2 of 2: Adverse Drug Reaction

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis is given intravenous tobramycin for a resistant urinary tract infection. Within hours she develops worsening ptosis, diplopia, and shallow breathing requiring respiratory support. Which of the following drug effects best explains this deterioration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antagonism of acetylcholine receptors producing neuromuscular blockade

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels in the phrenic nerve

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depletion of acetylcholine stores from presynaptic vesicles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased production of anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the motor end plate

explanation.summary: Aminoglycosides can rarely antagonize acetylcholine receptors and cause neuromuscular blockade.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rarely, aminoglycosides antagonize acetylcholine receptors, leading to neuromuscular blockade, so caution is advised in patients with myasthenia gravis. In myasthenia gravis, antibodies already interrupt acetylcholine binding at the receptor, and an aminoglycoside blockade directly compounds that existing deficit.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The effect described is at the acetylcholine receptor, not at nerve sodium channels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aminoglycosides act on the receptor rather than by depleting presynaptic acetylcholine stores.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aminoglycosides are not described as increasing autoantibody production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition would increase acetylcholine at the junction and improve, not worsen, weakness.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitors–2 of 2: Adverse Drug Reaction

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman reports drooping eyelids and weakness of her arms that worsens the longer she uses them and improves with rest. Which of the following best describes the underlying defect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies that block acetylcholine binding to its receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against skeletal muscle actin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degeneration of anterior horn motor neurons

choices.label: D
choices.text: Demyelination of peripheral motor nerves

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of acetylcholine release from the presynaptic terminal

explanation.summary: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies interrupt acetylcholine binding at its receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myasthenia gravis classically presents as muscle weakness that worsens with usage. Normally acetylcholine released from the nerve activates receptors on muscle to initiate contraction; in myasthenia gravis, antibodies alter those receptors and interrupt acetylcholine binding. This is the deficit that an aminoglycoside-induced neuromuscular blockade would compound.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The antibodies are directed at the acetylcholine receptor rather than at muscle actin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anterior horn cell degeneration describes a motor neuron disease, not myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Demyelination of motor nerves is not the lesion in myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The defect is at the postsynaptic receptor, not in presynaptic acetylcholine release.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitors–2 of 2: Adverse Drug Reaction

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman who is 16 weeks pregnant requires antibiotic therapy. Which of the following agents is most likely to be avoided in this patient because of the risk of fetal harm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Azithromycin, given orally

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clindamycin, given orally

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erythromycin, given orally

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gentamicin, given intravenously

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quinupristin/dalfopristin, given intravenously

explanation.summary: Aminoglycosides can cause fetal harm and are avoided in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside, and the brick states that aminoglycosides can cause fetal harm if given in pregnancy. Of the listed protein synthesis inhibitors, it is the one whose fetal risk is specifically highlighted.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azithromycin is a macrolide; fetal harm is not the adverse effect emphasized for this class.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clindamycin's listed adverse effects are diarrhea, allergic reaction and neuromuscular blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythromycin's concerns are hepatic metabolism, CYP3A4 interactions and QT prolongation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptogramins are associated with arthralgia/myalgia and laboratory abnormalities, not fetal harm.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitors–2 of 2: Adverse Drug Reaction

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is receiving amikacin for a resistant Pseudomonas infection, and the team wants to avoid adding a second nephrotoxic agent. Which of the following medications would most increase his risk of renal injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Azithromycin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clindamycin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Doxycycline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linezolid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vancomycin

explanation.summary: Concurrent nephrotoxic drugs such as vancomycin add to aminoglycoside renal risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists concurrent use of other nephrotoxic drugs as a risk multiplier for aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity, naming amphotericin B, polymyxins, NSAIDs, radiocontrast dye and vancomycin. Adding vancomycin to amikacin therefore compounds the tubular injury risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azithromycin's key concerns are CYP3A4 interactions and QT prolongation, not renal toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clindamycin is associated with diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis rather than nephrotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxycycline is linked to GI symptoms and photosensitivity, not renal injury.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Linezolid causes bone marrow suppression, peripheral neuropathy and serotonin syndrome.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitors–2 of 2: Adverse Drug Reaction

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman begins oral tetracycline for acne and asks what side effects are most likely. Which of the following should she be told is the most common problem with this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Easy bruising and mucosal bleeding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea

choices.label: C
choices.text: Numbness and tingling of the feet

choices.label: D
choices.text: Painful joints and aching muscles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ringing in the ears and hearing loss

explanation.summary: Tetracyclines are generally well tolerated but commonly cause gastrointestinal upset.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tetracyclines are considered generally safe, and their most common adverse reactions are gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. Counseling patients that these may occur, and asking them to report if the symptoms become a problem, is part of routine advice when starting the drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleeding from blood dyscrasias suggests chloramphenicol or linezolid marrow toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peripheral neuropathy is characteristic of prolonged linezolid therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arthralgia and myalgia are the hallmark of the streptogramins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tinnitus and hearing loss point to aminoglycoside ototoxicity, not tetracyclines.

questions.topicName: Protein Synthesis Inhibitors–2 of 2: Adverse Drug Reaction

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is given a 3-week course of tetracycline. Two years later his erupting permanent teeth show permanent yellow discoloration, and his growth has lagged. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The drug chelates calcium and deposits in calcifying teeth and bone

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug directly inhibits ribosomes inside mature ameloblasts

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug induces enamel-degrading matrix metalloproteinases

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug is oxidized to a yellow pigment within saliva

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug stimulates melanocytes located within the dental pulp

explanation.summary: Tetracyclines chelate calcium and deposit in calcifying teeth and bone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tetracyclines other than doxycycline deposit in calcifying teeth and bone, which discolors teeth yellow and can stunt growth in children. The mechanism is chelation, in which the drug binds calcium. This is why tetracyclines are contraindicated in children younger than 8 years.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The dental effect is due to calcium chelation and deposition, not host ribosomal inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enzymatic degradation of enamel is not how tetracyclines discolor teeth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Salivary oxidation to a pigment is not the described mechanism of staining.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Melanocyte stimulation in the pulp is not a described tetracycline effect.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with 2 days of dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. She is afebrile, and examination shows mild suprapubic tenderness without costovertebral angle tenderness. A urine culture is obtained before empiric therapy is begun. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be recovered?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enterococcus faecalis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Escherichia coli

choices.label: C
choices.text: Klebsiella pneumoniae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proteus mirabilis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Staphylococcus saprophyticus

explanation.summary: Acute cystitis is primarily caused by Escherichia coli.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute cystitis is an infection of the lower urinary tract, and it is primarily caused by Escherichia coli. E. coli is a gram-negative rod of the Enterobacteriaceae family, the group that typically causes urinary tract infections. Her afebrile presentation with suprapubic tenderness and no costovertebral angle tenderness is the classic lower-tract picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococci can cause acute cystitis but account for a minority of cases compared with E. coli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klebsiella is listed among the other organisms that can cause acute cystitis, not the most likely one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteus is also an occasional cause of acute cystitis but is not the predominant pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a recognized cause of acute cystitis but is far less common than E. coli.
